title: Entropy and the Arrow of Time

cards.h: Why a film run backwards looks wrong
cards.b:
Watch a film of an egg falling and splattering, then run it backwards: you laugh, because it cannot happen. Yet Newton's laws work equally well in both directions. A ball bouncing backwards in time obeys the same laws.

So what makes the past different from the future? The answer is entropy, and it is one of the deepest ideas in physics: the arrow of time comes from the way things spread out.

The word entropy was coined by Rudolf Clausius in 1865. Loosely, entropy measures how spread out energy is, or how many ways the parts of a system can be arranged without changing how it looks overall.

A tidy deck of cards has few arrangements. A shuffled deck has an astronomical number. Shuffling raises entropy. Hot coffee cooling into a room spreads its energy over many more molecules: entropy rises.

Ludwig Boltzmann (1870s) gave the precise meaning:

Boltzmann's entropy

S = k x ln(W)

W is the number of microscopic arrangements (microstates) that give the same large-scale look; k is Boltzmann's constant, 1.38 x 10 to the power -23 J/K; ln is the natural logarithm. This formula is engraved on his tombstone in Vienna.

More ways means higher entropy. Nature is not driven to disorder by a force; disorder simply has overwhelmingly more ways to happen.

The entropy of an isolated system never decreases. It rises in all real processes, and stays the same only in ideal, perfectly reversible ones.

For heat Q flowing at temperature T, the entropy change is Q / T. Heat leaving a hot body lowers its entropy a little; heat entering a cold body raises it more. The net is a gain, so heat flowing hot to cold is allowed and the reverse is not.

cards.h: Why the arrow of time exists
cards.b:
Imagine 100 gas molecules in a box, all in the left half. Opening a partition, they spread out. The chance that they all return to the left by themselves is (1/2) to the power 100, about 8 x 10 to the power -31. For a real gas, with 10 to the power 23 molecules, the odds are beyond zero for any practical purpose.

So the past is the direction in which entropy was lower. The question of why the early universe had such low entropy remains an open problem.

Living things are highly ordered, so do they break the law? No. A plant takes in low-entropy sunlight and gives off high-entropy heat. Earth's local order is paid for by a larger entropy increase elsewhere, mostly in the Sun's spreading light.

Looking far ahead, the universe may drift toward a state of maximum entropy, with all energy evenly spread, the so-called heat death. Physicists also link entropy to information: Claude Shannon's 1948 information theory uses a very similar formula.

1000 J of heat flows from a body at 400 K to one at 300 K.

Hot body loses entropy: -1000/400 = -2.5 J/K.

Cold body gains entropy: +1000/300 = +3.33 J/K.

Net change = +0.83 J/K, positive, so the process is allowed. Try the reverse (cold to hot): the net would be -0.83 J/K, negative, so it never happens on its own.

• 'Entropy just means messiness.' Useful as a picture, but the precise idea is counting microstates and the spread of energy.
  • 'Life violates the second law.' Only isolated systems must not lose entropy; living things are open systems.
  • 'Entropy can never decrease anywhere.' It can decrease locally (a freezer making ice) if more entropy is created elsewhere.

Satyendra Nath Bose's 1924 paper from Dhaka showed how to count the microstates of light particles correctly; Einstein translated and promoted it. The result, Bose-Einstein statistics, led to the idea of the boson, named after him, and to the Bose-Einstein condensate, first made in a lab in 1995.

Meghnad Saha used thermodynamics and statistics in 1920 to explain how atoms ionise in hot stars. The Saha equation lets us read the temperature of distant stars from their light.

• Entropy counts the ways a system can be arranged: S = k ln W.
  • The entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
  • This gives time its direction; it is statistics, not a force.
  • Local order, like life, is paid for by entropy increases elsewhere.

Think about it

1. Why does a stirred cup of milk and tea never un-mix?
2. A freezer lowers the entropy of water turning to ice. Where does the extra entropy go?
